interactions.summary: Jiang rejects a blanket command to quit jobs, says Dante would tell people to trust their own intuition, and even grants that if someone does not experience their condition as slavery then it may be acceptable for them.

A student asks Jiang to place Hamlet within Dante's moral map, and Jiang answers that Hamlet belongs in Purgatory rather than heaven because he killed Claudius, though the killing counts as justice rather than simple revenge.

A student tries to analogize enslaved or resigned people to the first sphere of heaven, and Jiang answers that Piccarda does not fit because she made a vow and was violently forced out of it rather than voluntarily abandoning her will.

claims.claim: Jiang says Dante would not give an absolute rule about modern jobs or servitude; the right action depends on a person's concrete situation and intuition.
claims.temporal_scope: Lecture explanation given on 2026-06-25 in response to a modern analogy.

claims.claim: He explicitly rejects absolute principles here, saying that Dante's judgment must be individualized rather than reduced to a single universal command.
Jiang says that if someone does not understand themselves as a slave, then their condition may be morally acceptable, but if they do experience it as slavery they should leave.
Jiang places Hamlet in Purgatory rather than heaven because Hamlet kills Claudius and therefore still needs repentance, even though his act is not mere vengeance.
claims.temporal_scope: Lecture explanation given on 2026-06-25 about Hamlet.

claims.claim: He argues that Hamlet turns vengeance into justice because he investigates Claudius's guilt and stages an open trial before killing him.
claims.temporal_scope: Lecture explanation given on 2026-06-25 through Jiang's reading of the play.

claims.claim: Jiang says Piccarda is not an example of surrendered free will because she vowed herself to God and was violently forced out of that vow by her brother.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang abruptly drops rule-based ethics and says there can be no absolute principles here, only intuition and situation.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there can be no absolute rule right there can be no principles
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharply qualifies the more severe anti-slavery claims in the preceding packets and keeps the lecture from flattening into simple legalism.

signature_moments.moment: The threshold becomes experiential: if you think you are being a slave, quit your job.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if you think you're being a slave then you should quit your job
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It translates Dante's freedom logic into a modern, subjective criterion.

signature_moments.moment: Hamlet's greatness lies in delaying revenge until he can convert it into justice.
signature_moments.source_phrase: turn the act of vengeance into an act of justice
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's cleanest interpretive formula and a strong reusable Jiang lens.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's refusal to turn Dante's free-will ethic into a universal social rule independent of individual intuition and circumstance.
Jiang's phrase for Hamlet's moral achievement when he investigates guilt and publicizes it rather than acting as a mere avenger.

glossary_terms.term: violently forced out of the vow
glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The criterion Jiang uses to distinguish coerced violation of a vow from voluntary surrender of free will.

chronology_notes.note: The packet complicates the previous hard line on slavery by introducing intuition and circumstance, then tests that flexible model against literary cases such as Hamlet and Piccarda.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's Hamlet summary compresses the play's details and should be treated as his interpretive classroom use of Hamlet rather than as a careful plot synopsis.
